specStatements.text: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
Students should be able to describe with examples where there are energy transfers in a closed system, that there is no net change to the total energy.
Students should be able to describe, with examples, how in all system changes energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways. This energy is often described as being ‘wasted’.
Students should be able to explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers, for example through lubrication and the use of thermal insulation.
The higher the thermal conductivity of a material the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.
Students should be able to describe how the rate of cooling of a building is affected by the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls.
Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.

Required practical activity 2 (physics only): investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation:
efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer)

(HT only) Students should be able to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Thermal conductivity appears in this topic only in the comparative form the specification itself uses: the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material. No defining equation is given, no unit is quoted, and no item asks for a value of thermal conductivity or for it to be substituted into a calculation. Items q07, q08 and q09 ask only which material or which wall transfers energy at the greater rate, and concept c07 states the comparison without defining the quantity.

concepts.definition: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy before a change is always equal to the total energy after it.
A system in which no energy enters or leaves. Energy can still be transferred between the stores inside a closed system, but there is no net change to the total energy of the system.
The spreading out of energy into stores that are less useful, most often the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is dissipated in all system changes.

The everyday name for energy that has been dissipated. It has not been destroyed; it has been stored in a way that cannot be used for the intended purpose, for example in the thermal store of a warm motor.
Putting a substance such as oil between surfaces that move over each other. The friction between the surfaces is reduced, so less energy is dissipated to thermal stores as the machine runs.
A layer of material of low thermal conductivity placed around an object or a building to reduce the rate of energy transfer by conduction to the surroundings.
A property of a material, used here only as a comparison: the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.

concepts.term: Rate of cooling of a building
concepts.definition: How quickly a building transfers energy to colder surroundings. The rate of cooling is lower when the walls are thicker and when the walls are made of a material with a lower thermal conductivity.

An investigation of the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators, and of the factors that affect the thermal insulation properties of a material, such as the thickness of the layer and the number of layers used.

concepts.term: Control variables in the insulation practical
concepts.definition: The quantities kept the same so that only the material or the thickness affects the result: the volume and starting temperature of the water, the size of the container, the room temperature and the time over which the temperature is measured.

concepts.term: AT 1 and AT 5 in this practical
concepts.definition: AT 1 is the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements of length, temperature and time; AT 5 is making measurements of energy and temperature changes. Both are exercised by measuring the thickness of the insulating layer with a ruler and by recording the fall in water temperature at set times.

Working scientifically and mathematical skills developed in this practical: taking repeat readings for each material, identifying anomalous results, calculating a mean temperature drop and plotting the results so that materials can be compared.

The share of the energy supplied to a device that is transferred usefully. The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). Efficiency is a ratio, so it has no unit and can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). Both powers must be in the same unit, and the answer is again a ratio with no unit.

Making a larger share of the input energy transfer useful by reducing the unwanted transfers: lubricating moving parts, insulating hot components, streamlining a moving object to reduce air resistance and using thicker wires of lower resistance.

misconceptions.question: A torch is left on until the battery is flat. What has happened to the energy?
misconceptions.correct: The same total energy still exists; it has been transferred to light and to thermal stores in the bulb and the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy has been used up, so there is less energy now than there was at the start.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks about a battery 'running out' of energy, and the useful effect really does stop, so the energy appears to have gone.
misconceptions.correction: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. The chemical store of the battery has emptied, but exactly the same total energy is now spread through the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the energy that a machine wastes?
misconceptions.correct: It is dissipated, which means it is stored in less useful ways, usually in thermal stores.
misconceptions.misconception: Wasted energy is destroyed once it has spread out into the surroundings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Wasted energy cannot be collected and reused, and it becomes impossible to detect once it is spread thinly, so students equate 'cannot be used' with 'no longer exists'.
misconceptions.correction: Dissipated energy is still there; it has simply been spread so thinly through the surroundings that it can no longer do anything useful.

misconceptions.question: A ball rolls to a stop in a closed system. What has happened to the total energy?
misconceptions.correct: There is no net change: the kinetic store has emptied into thermal stores inside the same system.
misconceptions.misconception: Friction lets some energy leak out of the system, so the total energy of the system falls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet friction as something that 'takes energy away' and do not notice that the thermal stores it fills are inside the boundary of the closed system.
misconceptions.correction: In a closed system nothing crosses the boundary. The energy has moved from the kinetic store to the thermal stores of the ball, the surface and the air, all of which are inside the system.

misconceptions.question: Can energy that has been dissipated to the surroundings be recovered?
misconceptions.correct: In practice it cannot; it is spread too thinly through the surroundings to be used again.
misconceptions.misconception: Dissipated energy is stored in the surroundings and will flow back into the device later on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are told that energy is never lost, and reason that anything which has not been destroyed must still be available for use.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation says the energy still exists, not that it is still useful. Once dissipated it is shared among a huge number of particles at a temperature close to that of the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: What does oiling the bearings of a machine do?
misconceptions.correct: It lowers the friction between the moving surfaces, so less energy is dissipated as the machine runs.
misconceptions.misconception: Oil removes friction completely, so a lubricated machine dissipates no energy at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oiled parts feel effortless to turn, and textbook problems often describe smooth surfaces as 'frictionless'.
misconceptions.correction: Lubrication reduces friction, it does not abolish it. Some energy is still dissipated to thermal stores, which is why no real machine is 100% efficient.

misconceptions.question: What does thick loft insulation do to a house?
misconceptions.correct: It lowers the rate of energy transfer through the loft, so the house cools more slowly.
misconceptions.misconception: Insulation stops energy escaping altogether, so an insulated house never cools down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'insulator' is heard as an absolute barrier, like a waterproof coat, rather than as something that slows a rate.
misconceptions.correction: Insulation reduces the rate of transfer; it does not stop it. An insulated house still cools, just more slowly than an uninsulated one.

misconceptions.question: Why does a room feel warmer after insulation is fitted?
misconceptions.correct: The energy from the heating stays in the room for longer, because it is transferred out more slowly.
misconceptions.misconception: The insulation gives out warmth of its own, which is why insulated rooms feel warmer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Insulating materials such as wool feel warm to the touch, because they conduct energy away from the skin only slowly.
misconceptions.correction: Insulation is not an energy source. It has no store to empty; it simply slows the transfer of energy out of the room.

misconceptions.question: A material has a high thermal conductivity. What does this tell you?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred across it by conduction at a high rate, so it is a poor insulator.
misconceptions.misconception: A high thermal conductivity means the material is good at holding energy in, so it insulates well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'conductivity' is read as a measure of how much energy the material can keep, and 'high' is assumed to be good.
misconceptions.correction: The higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material. Good insulators have a low thermal conductivity.

misconceptions.question: Two walls are built from the same brick, one thicker than the other. How do they compare?
misconceptions.correct: They have the same thermal conductivity, but the thicker wall transfers energy at a lower rate.
misconceptions.misconception: The thicker wall has a lower thermal conductivity, and that is why thick walls keep a building warm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thickness and conductivity both change the rate of transfer, so students merge the two into a single property of the wall.
misconceptions.correction: Thermal conductivity is a property of the material alone. Thickness is a separate factor: for the same material, a thicker wall gives a lower rate of transfer.

misconceptions.question: How does building thicker walls change the rate of cooling of a house?
misconceptions.correct: The house cools more slowly, because energy is transferred through the thicker wall at a lower rate.
misconceptions.misconception: Thicker walls make a building cool faster, because there is more material that has to be warmed up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly recall that more mass needs more energy to warm it, then apply that idea to the wrong quantity, the rate of transfer out of the building.
misconceptions.correction: The extra brick does have to be warmed, but the question is about the rate at which energy crosses the wall, and that rate falls as the wall gets thicker.

misconceptions.question: In the insulation practical, which material is the best insulator?
misconceptions.correct: The one whose beaker of water showed the smallest fall in temperature in the fixed time.
misconceptions.misconception: The best insulator is the one whose water cooled by the largest amount, because the most energy was involved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for the biggest number in the results table and assume that the biggest change means the best performance.
misconceptions.correction: A good insulator slows the transfer out of the beaker, so the water stays hot. The smallest temperature drop identifies the best insulator.

misconceptions.question: Which measurements must be recorded in the insulation practical?
misconceptions.correct: The thickness of the insulating layer, and the temperature of the water at set times.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the final temperature matters, because that is the reading taken at the end of the experiment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final reading answers 'how hot is it now', so students treat the readings taken along the way as unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: Cooling is a rate, so temperature must be recorded against time. AT 1 and AT 5 require appropriate apparatus for measuring length, temperature and time.

misconceptions.question: What must be kept the same when different insulating materials are compared?
misconceptions.correct: The volume and starting temperature of the water, the container, the room and the time allowed.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the material matters; the volume of water and its starting temperature can be left to vary.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students focus on the variable being investigated and forget that any other difference also changes the amount of cooling.
misconceptions.correction: Only the insulating material should differ. If the volume or the starting temperature changes as well, the comparison between the materials is no longer valid.

misconceptions.question: Why are repeat readings taken and a mean calculated in this practical?
misconceptions.correct: Repeats reduce the effect of random error, and a mean is a more reliable value than a single reading.
misconceptions.misconception: One reading is enough; repeating the measurement only makes the experiment take longer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first result looks like a perfectly good number, and the point of repeating is not visible unless the readings differ.
misconceptions.correction: Single readings scatter because of small random variations. Repeating and taking a mean reduces that scatter and lets anomalous results be spotted.

misconceptions.question: What makes the comparison between materials fair in this practical?
misconceptions.correct: Every beaker starts at the same temperature and is left for the same length of time.
misconceptions.misconception: To be fair, every material should be made to finish at the same final temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Fair test' is remembered as 'make everything the same', which is then applied to the outcome as well as to the conditions.
misconceptions.correction: The final temperature is the result, so it must be free to differ. What must be kept the same are the starting conditions and the time allowed.

misconceptions.question: How is efficiency calculated from energy values?
misconceptions.correct: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer)
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is the total input energy transfer divided by the useful output energy transfer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the equation is a fraction made from two energies but not which one goes on top, and dividing the bigger by the smaller feels safer.
misconceptions.correction: The useful output goes on top. Dividing the input by the output gives a number greater than 1, which cannot be an efficiency.

misconceptions.question: What does the efficiency of a device tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The share of the input energy transfer that ends up in the useful output.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency gives the fraction of the input energy that is wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lessons about efficiency dwell on wasted energy, so students attach the number to the waste rather than to the useful output.
misconceptions.correction: Efficiency counts the useful output. The wasted fraction is what is left over, so an efficiency of 0.3 means that 0.7 of the input is dissipated.

misconceptions.question: Can a device have an efficiency greater than 1?
misconceptions.correct: No. The useful output can never be greater than the total input, so efficiency is never above 1.
misconceptions.misconception: A very well made device can have an efficiency above 1, because it gives out more than it takes in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Percentages above 100% are common in everyday talk about improvement, and students do not connect efficiency back to conservation of energy.
misconceptions.correction: Energy cannot be created, so the useful output is at most equal to the input. Efficiency therefore lies between 0 and 1, or between 0% and 100%.

misconceptions.question: What unit does efficiency have?
misconceptions.correct: None. Efficiency is a ratio of two energies, or of two powers, so the units cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is measured in joules when energies are used, and in watts when powers are used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other quantity in the topic carries a unit, and the numbers substituted into the equation are in joules or in watts.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing joules by joules, or watts by watts, leaves a pure number. Efficiency is written as a decimal or as a percentage, with no unit.

misconceptions.question: How can the efficiency of a motor be increased?
misconceptions.correct: By reducing the unwanted transfers, for example by lubricating the bearings so less energy is dissipated.
misconceptions.misconception: Supplying more power increases the efficiency, because the motor then does more work each second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'more powerful' with 'better', and efficiency is assumed to be another word for performance.
misconceptions.correction: Efficiency is a ratio. Increasing the input raises the output as well, so the ratio barely changes; only cutting the wasted share raises efficiency.

misconceptions.question: Can a machine be made 100% efficient?
misconceptions.correct: No real machine is. Some energy is always dissipated, so efficiency can be raised but never reaches 1.
misconceptions.misconception: A machine that is oiled and insulated well enough wastes nothing and becomes 100% efficient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every method taught for improving efficiency reduces waste, so students extrapolate to a machine that wastes nothing at all.
misconceptions.correction: Friction and temperature differences can be reduced but not removed, so there is always some dissipation in a working machine.

mcqs.stem: A torch is left switched on until its battery is flat. What has happened to the energy that was in the chemical store of the battery?

options.text: It has been transferred to light and to thermal stores, so the total is unchanged.
options.rationale: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it has been transferred usefully and dissipated, leaving the total the same.

options.text: It has slowly been used up, so there is less energy now than at the start.
options.rationale: Students who hear that a battery 'runs out' believe the total amount of energy falls rather than moving elsewhere.

options.text: The part of it that was wasted has been destroyed inside the torch.
options.rationale: Wasted energy cannot be recovered, so students conclude that it has stopped existing.

options.text: It is stored in the bulb and is released again when the torch cools.
options.rationale: Students who know energy is conserved assume the dissipated energy is held somewhere, ready to be used again.

mcqs.stem: A ball bearing rolls along a bench and slowly comes to rest. The ball, the bench and the surrounding air are treated as a closed system. What is true of the total energy of this system?

options.text: It has fallen, because friction has let some of the energy leak out of it.
options.rationale: Friction is met as something that 'takes energy away', so students think a closed system loses energy overall.

options.text: It has fallen, because energy was used up in slowing the ball down.
options.rationale: Bringing something to rest looks like using energy up, rather than emptying one store into another.

options.text: It is unchanged; the kinetic store has emptied into the thermal stores.
options.rationale: In a closed system there is no net change to the total energy; the energy has only moved between stores inside it.

options.text: It has risen, because the friction has created extra thermal energy.
options.rationale: Students treat friction as a source of new energy rather than as a route by which energy moves between stores.

mcqs.stem: In every system change some of the energy is dissipated. What does dissipated mean?

options.text: The energy is stored in the surroundings and later returns to the system.
options.rationale: Students take conservation to mean that dissipated energy stays available and will return to the device.

options.text: The energy is stored in less useful ways, usually in thermal stores.
options.rationale: This is what the specification means by dissipation: energy ends up in stores that cannot do the intended job.

options.text: The energy is shared out equally between all the stores in the system.
options.rationale: 'Spread out' is read as 'shared equally', which describes sharing rather than dissipation.

options.text: The energy is destroyed as it spreads out into the surroundings.
options.rationale: Once energy is spread thinly it cannot be detected or used, so students say that it has gone.

mcqs.stem: A food mixer is running. Which energy transfer in the mixer is best described as ‘wasted’?

options.text: The transfer to the kinetic store of the rotating blades.
options.rationale: This is the useful output of the mixer; students who read 'wasted' as 'the largest transfer' choose it.

options.text: The transfer that is destroyed by friction in the bearings.
options.rationale: Friction does waste energy here, but students describe that waste as destruction rather than dissipation.

options.text: The transfer to the room that flows back into the mixer later.
options.rationale: Students who know energy is conserved assume the dissipated energy is on loan and will return.

options.text: The transfer to the thermal store of the warm motor.
options.rationale: Energy that warms the motor is dissipated: it is stored in a less useful way and cannot turn the blades.

mcqs.stem: The bearings of a machine are oiled regularly. Why does this reduce the unwanted energy transfers?

options.text: The oil takes in the wasted energy and stores it so it can be used again.
options.rationale: Students who know energy is conserved imagine the oil acting as a store that hands the energy back.

options.text: There is less friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal stores.
options.rationale: Lubrication lowers the friction between the moving surfaces, so a smaller share of the input is dissipated.

options.text: The oil removes the friction entirely, so no energy is dissipated.
options.rationale: Oiled parts turn very easily, so students treat lubricated surfaces as completely frictionless.

options.text: The oil makes the moving parts lighter and so easier to turn.
options.rationale: Students explain the easier movement by a change of weight rather than by a reduction in friction.

mcqs.stem: Thick insulation is laid in the loft of a house. Which statement about the house is now correct?

options.text: No energy can leave through the loft now, so the house never cools.
options.rationale: 'Insulator' is heard as a complete barrier, so students think the transfer is stopped rather than slowed.

options.text: The insulation gives out warmth of its own and heats the rooms up.
options.rationale: Insulating materials feel warm to the touch, so students treat them as a source of energy.

options.text: The building now cools down more slowly than it did before.
options.rationale: The insulation lowers the rate of energy transfer through the loft, so the building cools more slowly.

options.text: The energy is destroyed inside the insulating material.
options.rationale: Students who cannot trace where the energy goes conclude that the insulating layer removes it for good.

mcqs.stem: Two saucepan handles are the same size and shape, but one is made from a material with a higher thermal conductivity than the other. Which statement about that handle is correct?

options.text: It transfers energy by conduction at a higher rate than the other one.
options.rationale: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it.

options.text: It transfers energy more slowly, because it holds the energy inside itself.
options.rationale: 'Conductivity' is read as a measure of how much energy a material keeps, so high is taken to mean well insulated.

options.text: It transfers energy at the same rate, as the handles match in size.
options.rationale: Students who know that size affects the transfer assume that identical size makes the material irrelevant.

options.text: It must be thicker in order to conduct energy at that rate.
options.rationale: Thickness and conductivity are merged into one property, so a difference in conductivity is explained by thickness.

mcqs.stem: Two houses are identical except that one has thicker outside walls, built from the same brick. On a cold night, compared with the other house, the house with the thicker walls will

options.text: cool down faster, because there is more brick that has to be warmed up.
options.rationale: Students apply 'more mass needs more energy' to the rate at which energy leaves the building.

options.text: cool at the same rate, because the brick has the same conductivity.
options.rationale: Students who treat conductivity as the only factor conclude that thickness cannot matter at all.

options.text: warm itself up, because the thick walls give energy to the rooms.
options.rationale: Students who think insulating layers supply warmth extend the idea to thick brick walls.

options.text: cool down more slowly than the house with thinner walls.
options.rationale: For the same material, a thicker wall gives a lower rate of energy transfer, so the building cools more slowly.

mcqs.stem: An architect wants a new building to cool down as slowly as possible on a cold night. Which change should be made to its walls?

options.text: Build them from a material that has a higher thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Students who think a high conductivity means good insulation choose the material that conducts fastest.

options.text: Make them thinner so that less brick has to be warmed up first.
options.rationale: The 'more material to warm' idea leads students to think that thin walls slow the cooling down.

options.text: Make them thicker and use a material of lower thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Both factors act the same way: greater thickness and lower thermal conductivity each lower the rate of cooling.

options.text: Make them thinner and choose a brick that conducts more quickly.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think thin walls cool slowly and that a faster-conducting brick holds energy in.

mcqs.stem: In required practical activity 2, identical beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials and the water temperature is recorded for ten minutes. Which result identifies the best insulator?

options.text: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the smallest amount.
options.rationale: The best insulator gives the lowest rate of energy transfer, so its water stays hottest and drops least.

options.text: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the largest amount of all.
options.rationale: Students pick the biggest change in the results table and read it as the best performance.

options.text: The beaker whose water was the hottest when the timing started.
options.rationale: Starting temperature is a control variable, but students who ignore that read it as part of the result.

options.text: The beaker whose water ended at the temperature of the room.
options.rationale: 'Fair test' is remembered as making the outcomes match, so the beaker reaching room temperature looks right.

mcqs.stem: A student investigates how the thickness of an insulating layer affects the cooling of hot water in a beaker. Which measurements should be taken?

options.text: The temperature of the water at the end of the run, and nothing else.
options.rationale: The final reading answers 'how hot is it now', so students treat the earlier readings as unnecessary.

options.text: The temperature of the room, measured at the start and again at the end.
options.rationale: Room temperature is a control variable to check, not the measurement that shows how the water cools.

options.text: The thickness of the layer, and the water temperature at set times.
options.rationale: AT 1 and AT 5 are exercised here: the length is measured with a ruler and the temperature is recorded against time.

options.text: The mass of the insulation and the volume of the water used.
options.rationale: These are set-up details worth recording, but neither of them shows the rate at which the water cools.

mcqs.stem: The student repeats the cooling run three times for each material and calculates a mean temperature drop. Why is this done?

options.text: So that the water is given more time in which to cool down properly.
options.rationale: Students who see no point in repeats explain them as simply making the experiment last longer.

options.text: To reduce the effect of random error and give a more reliable result.
options.rationale: Repeat readings scatter because of random variation; a mean of several runs is more reliable and reveals anomalies.

options.text: To make every material finish at the same final temperature.
options.rationale: 'Fair test' is remembered as making everything the same, and is applied to the result as well as the conditions.

options.text: To change the independent variable several times over.
options.rationale: Repeating a run is confused with testing more values of the variable being investigated.

mcqs.stem: A small electric motor is supplied with 800 J of energy. Of this, 260 J is transferred usefully to a kinetic store. What is the efficiency of the motor?

options.rationale: 800 J divided by 260 J: the equation has been used upside down, giving a value greater than 1.
The 540 J of wasted energy has been divided by the 800 J input, giving the wasted share instead of the useful one.
260 J divided by the 540 J wasted: the useful output has been compared with the waste rather than with the total input.
efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer) = 260 J / 800 J = 0.325.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the efficiency of a device is correct?

options.text: A very well made device can have an efficiency of more than 1.
options.rationale: Percentages above 100% are common in everyday speech, and students do not link efficiency back to conservation.

options.text: The efficiency of a device can never be greater than 1.
options.rationale: The useful output energy transfer cannot exceed the total input energy transfer, so the ratio is at most 1.

options.text: Efficiency is measured in joules when energy values are used.
options.rationale: The numbers substituted are in joules, so students give the ratio the same unit as the quantities in it.

options.text: Efficiency gives the fraction of the input energy wasted.
options.rationale: Teaching about efficiency dwells on waste, so the number is attached to the wasted share of the input.

mcqs.stem: A motor has a total power input of 1200 W and a useful power output of 900 W. What is the efficiency of the motor?

options.rationale: 1200 W divided by 900 W: the equation has been inverted, giving an impossible efficiency above 1.
The wasted power has been worked out and quoted as the efficiency instead of the useful share.
The arithmetic is right but a unit has been added; dividing watts by watts leaves a pure number.
efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input) = 900 W / 1200 W = 0.75, a ratio with no unit.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A gearbox wastes energy because of friction between its moving parts. Which change would increase the efficiency of the intended energy transfer?

options.text: Lubricate the moving parts to reduce the energy dissipated.
options.rationale: Reducing an unwanted transfer leaves a larger share of the input as useful output, which raises the efficiency.

options.text: Supply more power to the gearbox, so that it does more work each second.
options.rationale: 'More powerful' is read as 'more efficient', but raising the input raises the output too, so the ratio hardly changes.

options.text: Remove the friction completely so the gearbox is 100% efficient.
options.rationale: Every method taught reduces friction, so students extrapolate to zero friction and perfect efficiency.

options.text: Run the gearbox for less time, so that less energy is wasted overall.
options.rationale: A shorter run wastes less energy in total, but the fraction of the input that is wasted is unchanged.
